l: Achilles, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles declares that he will not be appeased by Agamemnon son of Atreus or by the other Danaans, and that he will not accept Agamemnon’s gifts. He says he will not fight until Hector reaches the tents of the Myrmidons and attacks his ships.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Ulysses delivers the embassy’s appeal to Achilles and hears his refusal. He later reports to Agamemnon that Achilles remains fiercely angry, rejects the gifts, and intends to draw his ships into the water and advise the Achaeans to sail home.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Agamemnon son of Atreus is accused by Achilles of taking his prize, keeping much of the wealth won by others, and treating him with contumely. He sends Ulysses, Phoenix, and Ajax son of Telamon with gifts and promises, but Achilles refuses to be reconciled.

l: Phoenix, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Phoenix urges Achilles to overcome his anger and help save the Achaean ships, using his own history and the story of Meleager as examples. Achilles asks him to stay and sleep comfortably, but Phoenix remains with the embassy and plans to return with Achilles if he chooses to go home.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Ajax son of Telamon tells Ulysses that their mission to Achilles has failed and criticizes Achilles for being unforgiving. Achilles says that Ajax has spoken to his liking but confirms that he will not fight until Hector reaches the tents of the Myrmidons.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Hector is described as the force threatening the Achaeans and their ships. Achilles says that Hector formerly avoided fighting far from the walls when Achilles was present, and that he will not fight again until Hector reaches the Myrmidon tents and attacks the ships.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: The Danaans are represented by the embassy seeking Achilles’ help and offering gifts. Achilles says that they have received no greater benefit from fighting than from not fighting and tells them to find another plan for saving their ships and people.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: The Trojan people are said to have taken heart because Jove has protected Ilius. Achilles tells the Achaeans that they will not take the city while the gods continue to favor its people.

l: envoys, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: The envoys are Ulysses, Phoenix, Ajax son of Telamon, and the two heralds who accompany them. They return to Agamemnon’s tents and report that Achilles has refused the gifts and will not help the Achaeans.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Ilius is the city the Achaeans have failed to take and that Achilles says they will not reach as their goal. Its wealth before the Achaean arrival is used by Achilles as a comparison for the value of his life.

l: Troy, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Troy is referred to through the fighting around its walls and gates. Achilles says Hector once came to the Scaean gates and the oak tree but did not range farther while Achilles was fighting.

l: Agamemnon's gifts, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Agamemnon’s gifts include seven women, much other wealth, and promises of further rewards, including his daughter in marriage. Achilles rejects them, saying that even vastly greater gifts would not move him before he has been fully avenged.

l: Briseis, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Briseis is not named in this unit, but Achilles refers to the woman in whom he delighted and whom Agamemnon took from him. Achilles says he loved and cherished her and will not be reconciled while the wrong remains unavenged.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: The Achaean ships are threatened by Hector and by fire. Achilles says Agamemnon must rely on the other leaders to save them, while Phoenix warns that saving them will be harder once they are burning.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: The war has brought Achilles many hardships, including taking twelve cities by sea and eleven around Troy by land. Despite these efforts, he believes fighting brings equal honor to cowards and heroes and that he has received no adequate reward.

l: Achilles’ anger, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles’ anger remains fixed because Agamemnon took the woman awarded to him and insulted him before the Argives. Neither gifts, promises, arguments, nor the pleas of Phoenix and Ajax can persuade him to abandon it.

l: Agamemnon's insult and seizure of Achilles' prize, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles says Agamemnon took the woman he had won and thereby deceived and dishonored him. He treats this seizure as a bitter wrong that must be avenged before he can consider fighting again.

l: Achilles' choice of fates, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles says his mother Thetis told him that he has two possible fates: if he stays and fights, he will die but gain everlasting fame; if he returns home, his fame will die but he will live much longer. He emphasizes that life is worth more to him than all the wealth of Ilius.

l: Achilles' withdrawal from the war, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles plans to sacrifice to Jove and the other gods, draw his ships into the water, provision them, and sail toward Phthia if Neptune grants a fair passage. He says he may be there in three days and invites Phoenix to accompany him, though he will not force him.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Agamemnon and Menelaus remain awake because Hector has inflicted severe losses on the Achaeans, and they seek counsel and rouse the leaders. Agamemnon, Nestor, Ulysses, Diomed, and other chiefs inspect the watches and hold a council outside the trench. Diomed chooses Ulysses as his companion for a night reconnaissance among the Trojans. After praying to Pallas Minerva, they arm themselves and set out through the night.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Ulysses is roused by Nestor and joins the other chiefs in inspecting the Achaean watches. At the council he offers to go on a night reconnaissance, and Diomed chooses him as his companion because he is daring, quick to understand, and favored by Pallas Minerva. He arms himself with a bow, quiver, and a boar’s-teeth helmet, prays to Minerva, and sets out with Diomed.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Diomed is awakened by Nestor and helps rouse Ajax and the son of Phyleus. At the council he volunteers to enter the Trojan camp and chooses Ulysses to accompany him. He receives a sword, shield, and bull’s-hide helmet, prays to Pallas Minerva, and sets out with Ulysses.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Agamemnon cannot sleep because he fears for the Achaeans and their ships after Hector’s successes. He summons Menelaus, goes to Nestor for counsel, orders Menelaus to call other leaders, and joins the night meeting. He authorizes Diomed to choose the best companion for the reconnaissance.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Menelaus also remains awake because he fears for the Argives who came to fight the Trojans for his sake. He arms himself, goes to Agamemnon, and is sent to call Ajax and Idomeneus and to rouse the men along the camp. He offers to join the night reconnaissance, but does not go when Diomed chooses Ulysses.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Nestor is awakened by Agamemnon and joins him in rousing the leaders and inspecting the sentinels. He leads the chiefs beyond the trench to a council and proposes sending a man into the Trojan camp to learn the enemy’s intentions. He encourages the watchmen to remain alert and warns them not to let sleep give victory to the enemy.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Hector has inflicted great destruction on the Achaeans in a single day and has turned the balance of the war toward the Trojans. His attack reached the Achaean ships before he withdrew at nightfall, and his actions cause Agamemnon and the other leaders to fear for the army.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The Achaeans are in grave danger after Hector’s assault and are uncertain whether the Trojans will remain by the ships or withdraw into Troy. Their leaders inspect the watches, hold a council, and send Ulysses and Diomed to seek information about the enemy.

l: Argives, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The Argives are described as being in extreme danger, with their life and death balanced on a razor’s edge. Their leaders are urged to remain watchful and to act together to protect the ships.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The Trojans are encamped close to the Achaean ships, on the brow of the plain. Their camp and intentions are the subject of the proposed night reconnaissance, since the Achaeans do not know whether they will stay by the ships or return within their walls.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Troy is represented by its nearby army and by the possibility that the Trojans may withdraw within their walls. The Achaeans seek information about whether the enemy will remain outside the city or retire into it.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The Achaean ships are threatened by the Trojan camp, which lies close to them after Hector’s attack. Agamemnon fears for the ships and the men defending them, while the leaders inspect the guards stationed around the camp.

l: night reconnaissance, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: A night reconnaissance is proposed to discover what the Trojans intend to do and whether they will remain by the ships or withdraw into Troy. Diomed and Ulysses are selected for the task, arm themselves, pray to Pallas Minerva, and set out.

l: council of the Achaean chiefs, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The Achaean chiefs hold their council beyond the trench in an open space clear of corpses. Nestor proposes sending a spy into the Trojan camp, and Diomed volunteers before choosing Ulysses as his companion.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The war has brought the Achaeans severe losses, especially through Hector’s attack, and has left their leaders fearful and uncertain. The chiefs respond by strengthening the watches and planning a reconnaissance of the Trojan camp.

l: the threatened destruction of the Achaean fleet, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: The danger to the Achaeans is described as extreme because Hector has devastated them and the Trojans are camped near the ships. Agamemnon, Nestor, and the other leaders seek counsel, maintain the watches, and send Ulysses and Diomed to gather information.

l: sleep and watchfulness, The Iliad, BOOK X.
s: Agamemnon and Menelaus cannot sleep because of their fear, while Nestor rouses the leaders and the sentinels. The guards are found awake and armed, and Nestor urges them not to let sleep overcome them lest the Trojans triumph.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector asks the Trojan princes and councillors for someone to scout the ships of the Achaeans and learn whether they remain guarded. Dolon volunteers in exchange for Hector’s oath that he will receive the bronze-bedizened chariot and horses of Achilles. Ulysses and Diomed intercept Dolon as he approaches the ships, pursue him, and capture him alive. Dolon reveals that Hector is conferring near the monument of great Ilus and that the Trojans rely on watchfires and sentinels, while their allied forces are asleep.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector calls the Trojan princes and councillors together and offers a great reward to anyone who will scout the ships of the Achaeans. He swears to give Dolon the chariot and horses of Achilles if Dolon completes the mission.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The Trojans are kept awake by Hector’s call and initially remain silent when he asks for a volunteer. They maintain watchfires and keep sentinels awake to guard their camp.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The Achaeans are camped by their ships, and Hector wants to learn whether they still maintain their watches or are preparing to flee after being beaten.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The ships of the Achaeans are the destination of Dolon’s scouting mission. Hector wants information about whether they remain guarded.

l: Dolon, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Dolon, son of Eumedes, volunteers to scout the Achaean ships in return for the chariot and horses promised by Hector. He travels through the night but is pursued and captured by Ulysses and Diomed, after which he reveals information about the Trojan camp and its guards.

l: chariot, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector promises Dolon a bronze-bedizened chariot as a reward for scouting the Achaean ships.

l: horses of Achilles, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector swears that Dolon will receive the horses of Achilles. Ulysses tells Dolon that these horses are difficult for any mortal other than Achilles to keep in hand or drive.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Ulysses notices Dolon approaching and directs Diomed in the plan to intercept him. He questions Dolon after the capture and learns why he came, where Hector is, and how the Trojan and allied forces are guarded.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Diomed joins Ulysses in pursuing Dolon toward the Achaean ships. He throws his spear over Dolon’s shoulder on purpose, then helps seize him.

l: Trojan camp, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The Trojan camp is behind Dolon as he runs toward the ships, and Ulysses and Diomed work to prevent him from returning to it. Dolon reports that Hector and the councillors are conferring near the monument of great Ilus.

l: Trojan guards, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The Trojan guards use watchfires and remain awake to keep one another to their duty as sentinels. Dolon says there is no specially chosen watch guarding the host.

l: allies, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The allies who came from other places are asleep rather than keeping watch. They rely on the Trojans to guard the camp because their wives and children are not there.

l: the Trojan night watch, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector wants Dolon to determine whether the Achaeans are still maintaining their watches. Dolon reports that the Trojans keep watch through fires and sentinels, while the allied forces sleep.

l: scouting mission, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: The scouting mission is proposed by Hector to discover whether the Achaean ships are guarded and whether the Achaeans plan to flee. Dolon undertakes it for the promised chariot, horses, and honour, but he is captured before returning with news.

l: pursuit of Dolon, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Ulysses and Diomed hide among the corpses, let Dolon pass, and then pursue him toward the ships. They cut him off from the Trojan camp and capture him alive.

l: Trojan plans, The Iliad, Neither again did Hector let the Trojans sleep; for he too called
s: Hector and the other Trojan councillors are holding a conference near the monument of great Ilus. Dolon is asked whether the Trojans will remain by the ships or retire within their walls, but the text does not give an answer to that question.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Ulysses and Diomed question Dolon, learn where the Thracians are camped, and kill Dolon after he gives them information. They raid the sleeping Thracian camp, kill Rhesus and twelve of his soldiers, and seize his horses. Minerva urges Diomed and Ulysses to return before the Trojans can respond, while Apollo rouses the Trojan camp. The two heroes reach the ships of the Achaeans, where they wash, sacrifice to Minerva, and celebrate their return.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Ulysses questions Dolon about the positions of the Trojan forces and learns that the Thracians lie apart at the far end of the camp. He hangs Dolon's equipment on a tamarisk tree as an offering to Minerva, helps clear the bodies so the horses can pass, unties and drives off Rhesus's horses, and returns with Diomed to the ships of the Achaeans.

l: Dolon, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Dolon tells Ulysses and Diomed where the different forces are located and describes Rhesus, his horses, and his chariot. Although he asks to be spared or bound until his information can be tested, Diomed kills him.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Diomed kills Dolon after deciding that he cannot safely be released. He then kills Rhesus and twelve Thracian soldiers, follows Minerva's warning to return, and reaches the ships of the Achaeans with Ulysses.

l: Rhesus son of Eioneus, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Rhesus son of Eioneus is the king of the Thracians newly arrived at the Trojan camp. He is sleeping beside his chariot when Diomed kills him, and his horses are taken.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Minerva receives Dolon's equipment as an offering and gives Diomed courage during the attack on the Thracians. She later warns Diomed to return to the ships before another god rouses the Trojans.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: The Achaeans welcome Ulysses and Diomed when they return with Rhesus's horses. They follow Ulysses to the quarters of Diomed and rejoice at the success of the raid.

l: Thracians, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: The Thracians lie apart from the other Trojan forces at the far end of the camp, with their armour arranged beside them and their horses nearby. Diomed attacks them while they sleep and kills their king and twelve of their soldiers.

l: Trojan camp, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: The Trojan camp is thrown into an uproar after Hippocoon discovers that Rhesus's horses are gone and the soldiers are dying. The people gather and wonder at the deeds of Ulysses and Diomed as the heroes escape toward the ships.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: The ships of the Achaeans are the destination of Ulysses and Diomed after the raid. At the ships, Dolon's blood-stained equipment is hung at the stern of Ulysses's ship for a sacred offering to Minerva.

l: Thracian sleeping-ground, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: The Thracian sleeping-ground is the separated camp at the far end of the Trojan forces. Ulysses and Diomed reach it, find the soldiers asleep in three orderly rows, and attack them.

l: Rhesus’s horses, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Rhesus's horses are described as exceptionally fine, strong, whiter than snow, and fleeter than any wind. Ulysses unties them, fastens them together, and drives them back to the ships of the Achaeans.

l: Rhesus’s chariot, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Rhesus's chariot is described as decorated with silver and gold, with his remarkable golden armour lying in it. Rhesus's horses are fastened to its topmost rim while he sleeps.

l: Dolon’s equipment, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Dolon’s equipment consists of a ferret-skin cap, a wolf-skin, a bow, and a long spear. Ulysses hangs these spoils on a tamarisk tree in honour of Minerva and later hangs them at the stern of his ship for a sacred offering.

l: Dolon’s execution, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Diomed executes Dolon by striking him in the middle of the neck with his sword. The blow cuts through both sinews, and Dolon's head falls into the dust while he is still speaking.

l: raid on the Thracian camp, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Ulysses and Diomed raid the Thracian camp while its soldiers sleep. They kill Rhesus and twelve of his men, seize Rhesus's horses, and escape before the Trojan forces can stop them.

l: slaughter of the Thracian soldiers, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Diomed kills twelve Thracian soldiers in addition to Rhesus, striking them right and left as Minerva gives him courage. Their armour lies beside them, and the earth becomes red with their blood.

l: return to the Achaean ships, The Iliad, Ulysses then said, “Now tell me; are they sleeping among the / “I will tell you truly all,” replied Dolon. “To the seawa
s: Ulysses and Diomed return to the Achaean ships with Rhesus's horses and Dolon's spoils. The Achaeans welcome them, and the two heroes wash, anoint themselves with oil, and make a drink-offering of wine to Minerva.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Jove sends Discord to the Achaean ships, and she inspires the Achaeans to fight. Agamemnon leads the Achaeans in a powerful assault, killing many Trojans and driving them toward the city until Iphidamas and Coon wound him, forcing him to withdraw. Jove instructs Iris to tell Hector to hold back until Agamemnon is wounded, after which Hector is to lead the Trojans against the Achaeans. The Trojan ranks are routed before Agamemnon, but they turn and resist after he is wounded.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Agamemnon arms himself fully and leads the Achaeans into battle. He kills Bienor, Oileus, Isus, Antiphus, Pisander, Hippolochus, Iphidamas, and Coon, driving the Trojans toward the city. Coon wounds him in the arm, and when the pain becomes severe, Agamemnon boards his chariot and withdraws toward the ships.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Hector initially keeps away from the fighting while Agamemnon leads the Achaeans. After Iris delivers Jove’s message, Hector enters the battle, rallies the Trojans, and helps them turn back against the Achaeans.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Jove sends Discord to encourage the Achaeans and later watches the fighting from Mount Ida. He instructs Iris to tell Hector to wait until Agamemnon is wounded, promising Hector strength to kill the Achaeans until he reaches their ships and night falls.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: The Achaeans are encouraged by Discord and fight the Trojans with determination. Under Agamemnon’s leadership, they break the Trojan battalions and pursue them toward the city, but their advance is checked after Agamemnon is wounded.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: The Trojans first fight the Achaeans without either side gaining the advantage, then fall into a rout under Agamemnon’s attack. After Agamemnon is wounded, they turn back under Hector’s leadership and again meet the Achaeans.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: The battle begins with the Achaeans and Trojans fighting fiercely and evenly. Agamemnon then shifts its course by leading a devastating attack, but the fighting changes again when he is wounded and Hector rallies the Trojans.

l: Discord, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Jove sends Discord to the Achaean ships with the ensign of war. Standing beside Ulysses’ ship, she raises a loud cry that gives the Achaeans courage to remain and fight.

l: Iris, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Iris carries Jove’s message from Mount Ida to Hector. She tells him to hold back while Agamemnon is dominant and to attack once Agamemnon has been wounded.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: The Achaean ships are the place where the army is gathered and where Discord takes her stand. Ulysses’ ship is described as being in the middle of the line, with the ships of Ajax and Achilles at opposite ends; Agamemnon later orders the Achaeans to defend the ships.

l: Agamemnon’s wound, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: Agamemnon’s arm is pierced below the elbow by Coon’s spear. He continues fighting and kills Coon, but the wound later causes severe pain and forces him to leave the battle in his chariot.

l: the Trojan rout, The Iliad, BOOK XI.
s: The Trojan rout begins when Agamemnon breaks their battalions and pursues them toward the Scaean gates and the city. Many Trojans are killed or thrown from their chariots, and abandoned horses draw empty chariots through the fighting.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Hector son of Priam rallies the Trojans and Lycians, then kills many Achaeans and drives them toward the ships. Ulysses and Diomed son of Tydeus briefly check the Trojan advance, but Diomed is wounded by Alexandrus and withdraws, leaving Ulysses surrounded until Menelaus and Ajax son of Telamon rescue him. Hector later helps rout the Achaeans, while Ajax is forced to retreat under Jove's influence but continues to protect the Achaeans' ships. Alexandrus wounds Machaon, whom Nestor son of Neleus carries away from the fighting, and Eurypylus son of Euaemon helps defend Ajax before being wounded himself.

l: Hector, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Hector rallies the Trojans and Lycians after Agamemnon leaves the field, kills numerous Achaean chieftains and other fighters, and drives the Achaeans toward their ships. Diomed's spear strikes his helmet without wounding him, and Hector briefly falls to his knees before recovering and escaping in his chariot. He later returns to the fighting, makes great slaughter near the Scamander, and helps throw the Danaans into confusion, though he avoids fighting Ajax son of Telamon.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: The Trojans are urged by Hector to attack bravely and initially drive the Achaeans back. They suffer losses from Ulysses, Diomed son of Tydeus, and Ajax son of Telamon, but later surround Ulysses and pursue Ajax when Jove causes fear to seize him.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: The Achaeans are thrown into panic by Hector's attack and nearly flee to their ships. Ulysses, Diomed son of Tydeus, Menelaus, Ajax son of Telamon, and others temporarily rally them, but Hector and the Trojans continue to press them hard.

l: Jove, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Jove grants Hector a great triumph and causes the Trojans to gain the advantage at several points. He later ordains that neither side should have the advantage, and strikes fear into Ajax son of Telamon so that Ajax retreats.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Ulysses urges Diomed son of Tydeus to stand against Hector and kills several Trojans. He is wounded through the side by Socus, kills Socus, and then calls repeatedly for help when the Trojans surround him. Menelaus and Ajax come to his rescue and lead him out of danger.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Diomed stands with Ulysses against the Trojan advance, kills Thymbraeus, and helps kill the sons of Merops and Agastrophus. He throws a spear at Hector, but Hector's helmet turns it aside. Alexandrus shoots Diomed through the right foot, after which Diomed withdraws to the ships.

l: Alexandrus, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Alexandrus shoots Diomed son of Tydeus through the right foot while Diomed is stripping Agastrophus's armour, then taunts him. He later wounds Machaon son of Aesculapius in the right shoulder and wounds Eurypylus son of Euaemon in the right thigh.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Menelaus hears Ulysses calling for help and asks Ajax son of Telamon to join him in rescuing Ulysses. He helps bring Ulysses out of the press by taking him by the hand while his squire brings up Ulysses's chariot.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Ajax rescues Ulysses with Menelaus and then kills Doryclus while wounding several other Trojans. Jove causes fear to seize him, forcing him to retreat before the Trojans, but he repeatedly turns to hold them back and prevents them from reaching the Achaeans' ships. Eurypylus son of Euaemon rallies others to defend him when he is being overwhelmed by arrows.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Nestor follows Idomeneus's advice, mounts his chariot, takes Machaon son of Aesculapius with him, and drives toward the ships to remove Machaon from danger.

l: Idomeneus, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Idomeneus sees that Machaon has been wounded and tells Nestor son of Neleus to carry him away, explaining that a physician is worth many other men.

l: Machaon, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Machaon is wounded in the right shoulder by a triple-barbed arrow shot by Alexandrus. Nestor son of Neleus takes him by chariot toward the ships so that he will not be captured.

l: Eurypylus, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Eurypylus helps Ajax by killing Apisaon and stripping the armour from him. Alexandrus then shoots Eurypylus in the right thigh, forcing him to withdraw under cover while he calls the Danaans to defend Ajax.

l: Argives, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: The Argives are described as panic-stricken when Hector advances, leaving Ulysses without support. They later respond to Eurypylus's call and gather around him and Ajax, raising their shields to provide cover.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: The Achaeans nearly flee to their ships, and the Trojans repeatedly threaten to reach and take them. Ajax son of Telamon's retreat is limited because he continues preventing the Trojans from making their way to the ships.

l: shield, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: A shield turns aside or stops several attacks in the fighting. Ulysses's shield is pierced by Socus's spear, while Ajax's broad shield protects him as he retreats and blocks the Trojans.

l: spear, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Spears are used repeatedly by both sides. Diomed's spear strikes Hector's helmet without wounding him, Ulysses kills Socus with his spear, and Eurypylus uses his spear to kill Apisaon.

l: arrows, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Alexandrus uses arrows to wound Diomed son of Tydeus, Machaon son of Aesculapius, and Eurypylus son of Euaemon. A rain of Trojan arrows helps overpower Ajax son of Telamon.

l: battle, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: The battle shifts repeatedly as Hector leads the Trojans forward, Ulysses and Diomed briefly resist, and Ajax later holds back the Trojan advance. Fighting is especially fierce near the Scamander and around the Achaeans' ships.

l: wounding of Diomed, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Diomed is wounded when Alexandrus shoots an arrow through the flat of his right foot and fixes it in the ground. After drawing out the arrow with Ulysses covering him, Diomed mounts his chariot and returns to the ships.

l: rescue of Ulysses, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: When Ulysses is surrounded and wounded by Socus, he calls three times for help. Menelaus and Ajax son of Telamon break through to him; Ajax drives off the Trojans while Menelaus leads Ulysses away to his chariot.

l: wounding of Machaon, The Iliad, When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the
s: Alexandrus wounds Machaon son of Aesculapius in the right shoulder with a triple-barbed arrow. Fearing that the Trojans will capture him, Idomeneus orders Nestor son of Neleus to carry him toward the ships.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Achilles sees Nestor carrying the wounded Machaon away and sends Patroclus to learn what has happened. Nestor tells Patroclus that many Achaean leaders are wounded and urges him to persuade Achilles to send help, possibly by entering battle in Achilles' armor. On his way back, Patroclus encounters the wounded Eurypylus, takes him to a tent, removes the arrow, and treats the wound with warm water and herbs. Nestor also reminds Patroclus of the counsel that Menoetius and Peleus once gave to him and Achilles.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Achilles watches the fighting from the stern of his ship and sees Nestor carrying the wounded Machaon away. He sends Patroclus to ask about the wounded man, but Nestor criticizes him for keeping his valor to himself and refusing to help the hard-pressed Achaeans.

l: Patroclus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Patroclus obeys Achilles and goes to Nestor's tent to learn who has been wounded. After hearing Nestor's appeal, he runs back toward Achilles, but stops to help the wounded Eurypylus, whom he carries into a tent and treats.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Nestor brings the wounded Machaon from the battle and tends to him in his tent with food and drink. He tells Patroclus that Diomed, Ulysses, Agamemnon, Eurypylus, and Machaon are wounded, and urges him to persuade Achilles to send help. Nestor recounts his own youthful victory over the Epeans and reminds Patroclus of the instructions once given by Menoetius and Peleus.

l: Machaon, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Machaon, son of Aesculapius and shepherd of his people, is wounded and is carried out of the fighting by Nestor. He rests with Nestor in the tent, while Nestor says that Machaon is himself in need of healing.

l: Eurypylus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Eurypylus is wounded in the thigh by an arrow and limps away from the fighting near the ships of Ulysses. He asks Patroclus to remove the arrow and treat the wound, and Patroclus carries him into a tent and gives him aid.

l: Menoetius, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Menoetius once charged Patroclus to counsel and guide Achilles wisely, saying that Achilles was the better man but that Patroclus was older. Nestor reminds Patroclus that he has forgotten this charge.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: The Achaeans are under severe pressure, with many of their leading warriors wounded and little time to recover. Nestor fears that they will perish at their ships unless Achilles or Patroclus brings them help.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: The Trojans are growing stronger as the Achaeans' leading warriors lie wounded. Nestor proposes that Patroclus enter the fight in Achilles' armor so the Trojans may mistake him for Achilles and withdraw.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: The Achaean ships and tents are threatened by the fighting, and Achilles watches the battle from his ship. Nestor warns that the ships may be set ablaze while the Achaeans perish, while Patroclus moves among the ships and tents on his errands.

l: the Trojan assault on the Achaean ships, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: The Trojan attack has placed the Achaeans and their ships in great danger. Nestor says that the Achaeans are hard pressed and may see their ships burned unless help is sent.

l: the wounding of the Achaean leaders, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: The leading Achaean warriors have been struck down or wounded: Diomed, Ulysses, Agamemnon, Eurypylus, and Machaon are specifically named. Nestor uses their condition to urge Patroclus to persuade Achilles to intervene.

l: Patroclus treating Eurypylus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Patroclus carries Eurypylus into a tent, lays him on bullock-skins, and cuts the arrow from his thigh. He washes the wound with warm water and applies a crushed herb associated with Achilles, after which the wound dries and stops bleeding.

l: the counsel of Menoetius and Peleus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Peleus had charged Achilles to fight among the foremost and surpass his peers. Menoetius had charged Patroclus to guide Achilles wisely, and Nestor urges Patroclus to remember both instructions.

l: Achilles' refusal to fight, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. Meanwhile the
s: Achilles remains apart from the fighting and watches from his ship instead of entering the battle. Nestor condemns him for keeping his valor to himself and showing no concern for the wounded and endangered Achaeans.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Trojans and their allies, led by Hector, Polydamas, and Sarpedon, attack the Achaean trench, wall, and gates while the Achaeans defend their ships. Polydamas interprets an eagle dropping a blood-red snake as a warning, but Hector rejects the omen and continues the assault. Sarpedon and Glaucus lead the Lycians against the wall, where Ajax son of Telamon and Teucer reinforce Menestheus and the defenders. The Trojans tear down parts of the wall’s breastworks and battlements, and Sarpedon creates a breach by pulling away a battlement.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Achaeans are driven back to their ships and forced to defend the wall, gates, and battlements against the Trojan assault. Though discomfited and cowed by Jove, they continue resisting, encouraged by the two Ajaxes.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Trojans advance against the Achaean wall in organized companies after following Polydamas’s advice to fight on foot. Under Hector’s leadership, they tear down defenses and press toward the ships despite strong resistance.

l: Trojans and their allies, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Trojans and their allies assemble in five bodies under Hector, Paris, Helenus and Deiphobus, Aeneas, and Sarpedon. They charge the Achaeans, attack the wall and gates, and seek to break through to the ships.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Achaean wall remains under heavy attack as Trojans strike its timbers, breastworks, battlements, and buttresses. The wall is eventually breached when Sarpedon pulls away a battlement, although the Achaeans continue defending it.

l: trench, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The trench frightens the Trojan horses because of its width, overhanging banks, and sharp stakes. The Trojan infantry hesitate to cross it after seeing the eagle and snake, but Hector orders them onward.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Achaean ships are the object of the Trojan attack, and the Achaeans are forced back toward them. The Trojans hope to break through the wall and set the ships on fire.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Jove sends a mighty wind from Mount Ida that drives dust toward the ships, lulls the Achaeans into security, and gives victory to Hector and the Trojans. He also intends to give glory to Hector and has earlier shown the Trojans signs that encourage their attack.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Hector dismounts after accepting Polydamas’s advice that the Trojans should cross the trench on foot, and he leads the attack against the wall. He rejects Polydamas’s interpretation of the eagle and snake, insisting that the Trojans trust Jove and fight for their country.

l: Polydamas, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Polydamas advises the Trojans to leave their horses at the trench and attack the wall on foot. After seeing the eagle drop the snake, he interprets the sign as a warning that the Trojans may break through but will suffer losses and fail to return in order.

l: Sarpedon, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Sarpedon leads the allied Lycians with Glaucus and Asteropaeus and urges Glaucus to fight at the front because their honors and privileges require them to bear the brunt of battle. He attacks the wall, kills Alcmaon, and pulls away a battlement, creating a breach.

l: Glaucus, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Glaucus leads the Lycians alongside Sarpedon and accepts Sarpedon’s call to fight at the front. Teucer wounds him in the shoulder with an arrow, causing him to withdraw covertly from the fighting.

l: eagle carrying a snake, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: An eagle flies along the left wing of the Trojan host carrying a living blood-red snake in its talons. The snake strikes the eagle’s neck and breast, forcing it to drop the snake before flying away.

l: blood-red snake, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The blood-red snake struggles in the eagle’s talons and strikes it while still alive. After being dropped into the Trojan host, it writhes among them and becomes a source of terror.

l: omen of the eagle and snake, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Polydamas reads the omen as a warning that the Trojans may break through the Achaean wall but will not return safely, just as the eagle could not carry the snake home. Hector rejects this interpretation and refuses to let the omen stop the attack.

l: the two Ajaxes, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The two Ajaxes move along the wall, encouraging the Achaeans to stand firm and rebuking those who are remiss. They urge the defenders to press forward and keep one another’s courage up.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Ajax son of Telamon goes to Menestheus’s aid when the Lycians attack his section of the wall. He kills Epicles by throwing a large stone that crushes his helmet and head, then continues fighting with Teucer.

l: Teucer, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: Teucer accompanies Ajax son of Telamon to reinforce Menestheus and the threatened section of the wall. He wounds Glaucus in the exposed shoulder with an arrow, forcing Glaucus to withdraw.

l: battle for the Achaean wall, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The battle rages along the entire Achaean wall, with stones and weapons falling heavily on both sides. The Achaeans defend the wall and ships while the Trojans seek to tear down its defenses and force a passage.

l: Trojans' assault on the wall, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Trojans assault the wall in companies, attacking its gates, breastworks, battlements, and buttresses. Their attack gains ground when Sarpedon breaks a battlement and makes a breach, but the Achaeans continue to resist.

l: gates (Achaean wall's gates), The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Achaean gates are opened and their great bar is lowered so that fleeing Achaeans can enter. Asius attacks them with his horses, but Polypoetes and Leonteus defend the gates and kill several of his men.

l: breastworks and battlements, The Iliad, BOOK XII.
s: The Trojans tear down the breastworks, overthrow the battlements, and pull up the buttresses placed before the Achaean wall. Sarpedon seizes a battlement and pulls it away, opening a breach through which many Trojans might pass.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Ajax and Teucer attack Hector at the wall, but Jove saves his son from destruction. The Lycians and Argives struggle fiercely for control of the wall and battlements, with neither side initially able to prevail. Jove gives Hector greater glory, and Hector leads the Trojans in an assault that breaks through the gates. The Danaans flee toward their ships in panic and confusion.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Ajax attacks Hector and pierces his shield with a spear, though the spear does not pass through and forces Hector back from the battlement.

l: Teucer, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Teucer attacks Hector and strikes him with an arrow on the band bearing the shield that covers his body.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Jove saves his son from destruction so that he will not fall by the ships' sterns. He later gives greater glory to Hector.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Hector is struck by Teucer's arrow and driven back by Ajax, but he calls on the Lycians to support him. He then leads the attack on the wall, lifts a great stone, breaks open the gates, and enters through them, urging the Trojans to follow.

l: Lycians, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The Lycians draw closer around Hector after he rebukes them and fight the Argives for possession of the wall. They cannot initially break through the wall or force their way to the ships, but they follow Hector into the breach.

l: Argives, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The Argives arrange their men in fighting order within the wall and engage the Lycians in a deadly struggle. They hold the wall until Hector breaks open the gates.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The Danaans fight to hold the wall and battlements, but flee panic-stricken toward their ships after Hector enters through the gates.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The Trojans are urged by Hector to break the wall and set fire to the ships. They rush at the wall, climb over it or pass through the opened gates, and drive the Danaans into flight.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The Achaeans hold on and are not routed by the Trojans during the struggle at the wall. Their wall and battlements are covered with the blood of Achaeans and Trojans.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The ships are the destination toward which the Trojans seek to force their way and upon which Hector orders them to fling fire. The fleeing Danaans retreat toward them.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The wall is the main point of contention between the Lycians and the Argives. Hector leads the Trojans against it, and the fighting ends with the Trojans entering through the broken gates.

l: breastworks and battlements, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The battlements are contested by the Lycians and the Argives, who strike one another with spears and shields. Hector first springs toward them before breaking through the gates.

l: gates (Achaean wall's gates), The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The gates block the Trojans' way until Hector strikes them with a great stone and breaks them open. Afterward, Trojans enter both over the wall and through the gates.

l: the doors, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The doors at the gates are double and high, secured by two cross-bars and one key. Hector's blow breaks both hinges, causes the bars to fail, and sends the doors flying open in opposite directions.

l: the stone, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Hector lifts the large stone easily and drives it against the middle of the doors with his full weight. Its blow breaks the hinges and opens the gates.

l: battle for the Achaean wall, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The fighting at the wall is a deadly, closely balanced struggle between the Lycians and the Argives. Many men are wounded or pierced through their shields, and the wall and battlements are drenched with blood.

l: Trojans' assault on the wall, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: Hector commands the Trojans to attack the wall, break it, and set fire to the ships. The Trojans rush forward, scale the wall, and enter through the gates after Hector breaks them open.

l: the breaking of the gates, The Iliad, Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him
s: The breaking of the gates occurs when Hector strikes their double doors with a great stone. The hinges break, the cross-bars no longer hold, and the doors fly open, allowing Hector and the Trojans to enter.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Jove turns his attention away from Troy while Hector and the Trojans press their assault against the Achaean ships. Neptune, angered by the Achaeans’ danger, secretly intervenes by encouraging the two Ajaxes and other Achaean warriors, strengthening their resolve and organizing resistance. Hector’s advance is checked by the Achaean defensive formation, while fighting continues around the ships and causes losses on both sides. Neptune then urges Idomeneus into battle, and Idomeneus and Meriones lead a renewed attack against the Trojans.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Jove leaves Hector and the Trojans to their toil and turns his attention away from Troy, believing that no immortal will help either side. He intends to give victory to the Trojans and Hector in order to honor Achilles, but he does not intend to destroy the Achaean army completely.

l: Neptune, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Neptune watches the battle from Samothrace, pities the hard-pressed Achaeans, and grows furious with Jove. He travels from his palace beneath the sea to the Achaean ships, assumes human disguises, strengthens the Achaeans’ courage, and urges them to resist.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Hector leads the Trojans through the wall and gates toward the Achaean ships, driving forward like a storm or a falling rock. The Achaean defensive ranks check him and force him to give ground briefly, but he rallies the Trojans and continues the assault.

l: Idomeneus, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Idomeneus is urged by Neptune, disguised as Thoas, to return to the fighting. He arms himself, joins Meriones, and chooses to attack on the left wing, where he believes the Achaeans are weakest.

l: Meriones, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Meriones breaks his spear against Deiphobus’s shield and returns to his tent to fetch another. After arming himself, he joins Idomeneus and leads the way toward the left wing of the battle.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The Achaeans are in severe danger after the Trojans break through their wall and reach the ships. Neptune encourages them to recover their courage, and they form a dense defensive line that checks Hector’s advance.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The Trojans follow Hector in close formation, break through the Achaean wall and gates, and press toward the ships. They meet strong resistance from the Achaeans, suffer losses including Imbrius, and continue fighting fiercely around the ships.

l: Hector's Trojan force, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Hector’s force advances in a dense body toward the Achaean ships and initially appears capable of overrunning the tents and fleet. The force is halted by the closely packed Achaean battalions, though Hector urges the Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians to stand firm.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Ajax son of Telamon receives Neptune’s encouragement and feels greater strength and eagerness for battle. He helps form the Achaean defensive line, drives Hector back with a spear thrust against his shield, and helps carry Imbrius’s body from the fighting.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Ajax son of Oileus recognizes that Neptune has spoken to him in the likeness of Calchas and feels his hands and feet made more eager for battle. He throws a spear at Hector, helps carry away Imbrius, and cuts off Imbrius’s head in revenge for Amphimachus.

l: the two Ajaxes, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The two Ajaxes are encouraged directly by Neptune and gather strong bands of Achaeans around them. Their troops form a tightly packed wall of spears, shields, helmets, and men that checks Hector’s advance.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Achilles is not present in the described fighting, but Jove intends to glorify him by allowing victory to Hector and the Trojans.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Troy is the city toward which Jove turns his attention away while the fighting reaches the Achaean ships. The Trojans have sallied far from the city to fight at the ships.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The battle at the ships becomes a fierce close-quarters struggle after the Trojans break through the wall and gates. The combat includes dense formations, spear and sword fighting, and deaths on both sides.

l: Neptune's intervention, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: Neptune’s intervention consists of secretly entering the Achaean side in human disguises, encouraging the warriors, and increasing their courage and strength. He first aids the two Ajaxes and other Achaeans, then urges Idomeneus and Meriones to rejoin the fighting.

l: the Trojan assault on the Achaean ships, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The Trojan assault is led by Hector, who brings his forces through the Achaean wall and gates and toward the ships. The assault is checked by the Achaean defensive formation, though fighting continues under and around the ships’ sterns.

l: the Achaean defensive formation, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The Achaeans gather around the two Ajaxes in a tightly serried formation, with spear, shield, buckler, helmet, and man pressed closely together. This living fence prevents Hector from continuing easily through the tents and ships and drives him back for a time.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XIII.
s: The Achaean ships are threatened by Hector and the Trojans after the wall and gates are breached. The fighting takes place beside and beneath the ships, while the Achaeans struggle to prevent the Trojans from setting them on fire or capturing them.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Idomeneus leads a fierce Achaean attack, killing Othryoneus, Asius, and Alcathous while challenging Deiphobus. Deiphobus kills Hypsenor and wounds Ascalaphus, but Meriones wounds him and his brother Polites carries him from the fight. Aeneas joins the Trojans in fighting around Alcathous’s body, while Antilochus, Meriones, and others defend the Achaeans and recover their fallen. Menelaus kills Pisander, and further fighting leaves Harpalion, Euchenor, and several other warriors dead or wounded.

l: Idomeneus, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Idomeneus rallies the Danaans and drives panic among the Trojans. He kills Othryoneus, Asius, and Alcathous, boasts over them, challenges Deiphobus, and continues fighting despite growing fatigue and heavy missile fire.

l: Antilochus, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Antilochus kills the charioteer of Asius and drives the charioteer’s horses from the Trojans to the Achaeans. He helps protect Hypsenor’s body, later kills Thoon, and is protected from Adamas’s spear by Neptune.

l: Deiphobus, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Deiphobus comes to avenge Asius, but his spear misses Idomeneus and kills Hypsenor instead. He summons Aeneas to help him, wounds Ascalaphus while retreating, and is then wounded in the arm by Meriones and carried from the battle by Polites.

l: Aeneas, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Aeneas joins Deiphobus after being reminded that Alcathous, his sister’s husband, had raised him. He leads Trojan fighters against Idomeneus’s group, throws a spear that Idomeneus avoids, and kills Aphareus.

l: Meriones, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Meriones wounds Deiphobus in the arm and forces him to drop his helmet. He kills Adamas by stabbing him between the private parts and the navel, and later kills Harpalion with an arrow through the buttock.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Menelaus fights Helenus, wounds his bow hand, and later kills Pisander by striking him in the forehead. He denounces the Trojans for taking his wife and treasure and for attacking the Achaean ships.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: The Trojans fight fiercely around Alcathous’s body and follow Aeneas into battle. They suffer the deaths of Othryoneus, Asius, Alcathous, Aphareus, Thoon, Adamas, Pisander, Harpalion, and Euchenor, among others, while Deiphobus, Helenus, and others are wounded.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: The Achaeans are rallied by Idomeneus and fight to defend their position and recover their fallen. They suffer losses including Hypsenor, Ascalaphus, Oenomaus, Deipyrus, and Aphareus, but their fighters kill or wound many Trojans.

l: Troy, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Troy is the city for which the Trojans fight. Menelaus declares that Jove will one day destroy it because of the Trojans’ violation of hospitality and abduction of his wife.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: The ships of the Achaeans remain the threatened destination of the fighting. Menelaus says that the Trojans intend to fling fire upon them and declares that the Trojans will be driven away from them.

l: spear, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: Spears dominate the close combat: Idomeneus kills Othryoneus, Asius, and Alcathous with one; Deiphobus kills Hypsenor and wounds Ascalaphus; and many others are wounded or killed by spears. Neptune makes Adamas’s spear ineffective against Antilochus, leaving part of it stuck in the shield.

l: battle, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: The battle centers on furious close combat around the body of Alcathous and continues without pause. Warriors fight with spears, swords, bows, and axes, while bodies are defended, stripped of armor, or carried from the field.

l: the Trojan assault on the Achaean ships, The Iliad, And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with grey,
s: The Trojan assault threatens the Achaean ships with fire and the killing of their heroes. Menelaus condemns the Trojans for this attack, while the Achaeans continue resisting them in battle.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Hector continues attacking the Achaeans at the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus, unaware that Neptune is helping the Argives defeat the Trojans on the left wing. Polydamas advises Hector to gather the Trojan chieftains and consider either attacking the ships or retreating, and Hector goes to summon them. Hector finds Alexandrus, who reports that many Trojan leaders are dead or wounded, and the two join the fiercest fighting. Hector and Ajax son of Telamon exchange threats as the Trojans and Achaeans prepare for another assault.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Hector continues forcing his way toward the Achaean ships, where he is difficult to stop or drive back. He accepts Polydamas's advice to gather the Trojan chieftains, searches for missing leaders, rebukes Alexandrus, and then leads the Trojans into the thickest fighting.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The Argives are making havoc of the Trojan forces on the left wing, with Neptune encouraging and helping them. They kill Asius and Adamas near the Achaean ships and stand firm against the Trojan chieftains.

l: Argives, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The Achaeans fight fiercely to defend their ships and prevent Hector from advancing. They take heart when a bird flies on their right and raise a shout, then withstand the Trojan onslaught.

l: ships of Ajax and Protesilaus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The ships of Ajax and Protesilaus are drawn up by the sea-shore at the point where Hector first broke through the gates and wall. The wall is lowest there, and the fighting around the ships is especially fierce.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Ajax son of Telamon stands shoulder to shoulder with Ajax son of Oileus and bears the brunt of the fighting. His comrades relieve him of his shield when sweat and toil overcome him, and he challenges Hector to draw near.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The wall is lowest near the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus, making that place a center of fierce fighting. Hector has already forced his way through the wall after breaking through the serried ranks of the Danaan warriors.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Ajax son of Oileus never leaves the side of Ajax son of Telamon, and the two fight together like paired oxen. His Locrian followers remain farther back because they are equipped mainly with bows and slings rather than heavy armor.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The Trojans begin to lose heart when the Locrians' arrows throw them into confusion. They later regroup behind their leaders and advance in ranks toward the Achaeans, though they cannot daunt the Achaean courage.

l: Polydamas, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Polydamas criticizes Hector for believing that excellence in war makes him superior in counsel. He advises Hector to withdraw and gather the chieftains to decide whether to attack the ships or retreat, then gathers the leaders as Hector ordered.

l: Alexandrus, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Alexandrus, husband of Helen, is found on the left wing encouraging his men and fighting the Danaans. He tells Hector that Deiphobus and Helenus are wounded, that other comrades are dead, and that he will follow Hector as far as his strength permits.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Jove is invoked in the exchanges between Ajax and Hector. He urges the Trojans onward to fight, and Ajax's challenge predicts that Hector will one day pray to Jove and the gods while fleeing.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: Hector tells Alexandrus that Ilius is undone and will surely fall because of the losses among the Trojan leaders. Alexandrus replies that the Trojans have continued fighting around the ships.

l: battle, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The battle rages most fiercely near the lowest part of the wall and the ships. Its left wing favors the Argives, while the Trojans and Achaeans later confront one another in a renewed clash near the ships.

l: the Trojan assault on the Achaean ships, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The Trojan assault on the ships is led by Hector, with the Trojan chieftains following him in ordered ranks. Hector tests the Achaean lines under cover of his shield, but Ajax and the other Achaeans stand firm against the attack.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector
s: The ships are the main objective of Hector and the Trojans and the place where the Achaeans make their strongest defense. The fighting around them causes heavy losses among the Trojan leaders, including Asius and Adamas.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Agamemnon proposes withdrawing the Achaean ships into the sea, but Ulysses rejects the plan and Diomed advises the wounded kings to encourage the fighting men. Neptune strengthens the Achaeans, while the Trojans press their attack against the ships after the Achaean wall falls. Juno deceives Jupiter by obtaining Venus’s girdle and persuading Sleep to lull him, allowing Neptune to aid the Achaeans while Jupiter sleeps.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Agamemnon sees the Achaeans routed and proposes drawing the ships into the water and securing them offshore, arguing that it is better to escape ruin than be killed. Ulysses rebukes him, and Agamemnon accepts that others may offer better counsel before going with Nestor and Diomed to encourage the fighters.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Ulysses fiercely rejects Agamemnon’s proposal to draw down the ships, warning that the Achaeans would stop fighting if they saw the fleet being moved and that the plan would lead to destruction.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Nestor leaves Machaon in his tent and goes to investigate the fighting. After seeing the Achaeans routed and meeting Agamemnon, Ulysses, and Diomed, he agrees that the wall has fallen and that the wounded kings should consider what to do without entering the battle.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Diomed advises Agamemnon, Nestor, and Ulysses to go to the fight despite their wounds, remain beyond the range of the spears, and encourage those who have been holding aloof from battle.

l: Neptune, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Neptune approaches Agamemnon in the semblance of an old man and promises that the Trojan princes will again raise dust as they flee toward their city. He then gives a mighty battle cry that renews the Achaeans’ courage, and Sleep later tells him to aid the Danaans while Jupiter sleeps.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Jupiter is on the topmost crests of Mount Ida while the battle goes against the Achaeans. Juno arouses his passion, persuades him to lie with her, and causes him to fall asleep, leaving Neptune free to aid the Achaeans for a time.

l: Juno, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Juno is pleased when she sees Neptune aiding the Achaeans and devises a plan to deceive Jupiter. She obtains Venus’s girdle, asks Sleep to lull Jupiter, and persuades Jupiter to lie with her on Mount Ida so that Sleep can overtake him.

l: Venus, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Venus agrees to help Juno and gives her the embroidered girdle containing love, desire, and flattering charm. She then returns to Jupiter’s house.

l: Sleep, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Sleep initially refuses to lull Jupiter because Jupiter had previously punished him for helping Juno against Hercules. After Juno promises him Pasithea in marriage and swears by the Styx, Sleep hides on Mount Ida, puts Jupiter to sleep, and reports to Neptune that he can now aid the Danaans.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Achaeans suffer a disastrous rout after their wall falls, and the Trojans fight at their ships. Neptune’s battle cry restores their courage, and their wounded leaders go to encourage them while Jupiter sleeps.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Trojans attack stubbornly and without ceasing after the Achaean wall is overthrown, killing Achaeans in confusion and fighting at the ships. Neptune predicts that they will later flee from the ships and tents toward their city.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Troy is described as the city for which the Achaeans have suffered great hardship. Sleep recalls that Hercules once sacked the city of the Trojans before setting sail from Ilius.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Juno looks down from a peak of Olympus and later leaves its summit to carry out her deception. She tells Venus that she is going to the world’s end, though her real purpose is to distract Jupiter.

l: Ida, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Mount Ida is where Jupiter watches the battle and where Juno meets him. Juno and Sleep reach its forests, Sleep hides in a pine tree, and Jupiter and Juno lie together on its crest while a golden cloud conceals them.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The battle rages around the Achaean ships, with the Trojans pressing their attack and bronze weapons rattling against the fighters. Neptune’s cry strengthens the Achaeans, while the wounded kings go to the fighting to encourage others rather than fight directly.

l: Achaean retreat, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Achaeans are in a disastrous retreat, flying pell-mell before the Trojans. Agamemnon proposes withdrawing the ships as part of the retreat, but Ulysses rejects the idea and Diomed urges the leaders to support the fighting men.

l: destruction of the Achaean wall, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Achaean wall has fallen despite being relied upon as an impregnable defense for the army and fleet. Its fall leaves the Trojans fighting at the ships and contributes to the Achaeans’ rout.

l: Hera’s deception of Jupiter, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Juno deceives Jupiter by claiming that she is going to visit Oceanus and Tethys, obtaining Venus’s girdle, and arranging for Sleep to assist her. She then seduces Jupiter on Mount Ida, where Sleep causes him to fall into slumber.

l: the Trojan assault on the Achaean ships, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Trojan assault reaches the Achaean ships after the wall falls. The Trojans fight stubbornly at the ships, while the Achaeans are killed and driven into confusion.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Achaean fleet is drawn up along the shore, with the ships placed in rows because the bay cannot hold them all side by side. Agamemnon proposes drawing the ships into the water and mooring them offshore, but Ulysses warns that doing so during the battle would destroy the Achaeans’ will to fight.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: The Achaean wall and trench had been built as an impregnable bulwark for the army and fleet. The wall is overthrown, leaving the Trojans free to attack the ships.

l: Venus’s girdle, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Venus’s girdle contains love, desire, and sweet flattery that can steal the judgment of even the most prudent. Venus gives it to Juno, who places it in her bosom and uses its charms in her plan to beguile Jupiter.

l: counsel about retreat, The Iliad, BOOK XIV.
s: Agamemnon counsels drawing the ships into the water and escaping by night, but Ulysses condemns the proposal as destructive. Diomed instead counsels the wounded leaders to go near the battle and encourage the Achaeans while avoiding the spears.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Sleep departed, and Neptune rallied the Danaans to defend their ships against Hector son of Priam and the Trojans. The Danaans exchanged armour and advanced under Neptune, while Ajax son of Telamon struck Hector with a stone and forced him from the battle. Hector was carried to the ford of Xanthus, where he briefly recovered before falling back unconscious. The fighting continued with many deaths, including those of Satnius, Prothoenor, Archelochus, Promachus, and Ilioneus, as the Danaans gained the advantage.

l: Neptune, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Neptune became more eager than ever to help the Danaans after Sleep departed. He rallied them, led them into battle, and fought on their side with a terrible sword.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: The Danaans followed Neptune's instructions by exchanging armour so that their strongest fighters received the best equipment. They advanced against the Trojans, recovered their courage when Hector left the field, and attacked with greater fury.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Hector son of Priam arranged the Trojans and fought against Neptune and the Danaans. His spear failed to wound Ajax son of Telamon, and Ajax struck him with a stone, leaving him stunned and badly hurt.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Ajax son of Telamon was attacked by Hector's spear, but his shield and sword bands protected him. He then struck Hector above the rim of his shield with a stone, causing Hector to fall, and later killed Archelochus when his spear aimed at Polydamas went astray.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: The Trojans fought the Danaans under Hector's command and protected Hector after Ajax son of Telamon struck him down. Their warriors also suffered heavy losses as the Danaans pressed their attack.

l: Polydamas, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Polydamas son of Panthous avenged Satnius by wounding Prothoenor and boasting over him. He then tried to retreat from Ajax son of Telamon's attack, causing Ajax's spear to strike Archelochus instead.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Ajax son of Oileus killed Satnius son of Enops at the beginning of the renewed fighting. He later killed more men than any other fighter because he was the fleetest pursuer of the fleeing Trojans.

l: battle, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: The battle became extremely loud and fierce as the Trojans and Danaans met near the ships and tents. After Hector was removed from the field, the Danaans gained confidence and caused many Trojan and Danaan casualties.

l: Neptune's rallying of the Danaans, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Neptune urged the Danaans to support one another and resist Hector without waiting for Achilles. He told them to take the largest shields, put on their helmets, carry their longest spears, and exchange inferior armour for better equipment.

l: Hector's wounding and removal from battle, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: After Hector's spear failed against Ajax son of Telamon, Ajax struck him in the neck with a stone and knocked him down. Hector's comrades covered him with shields, carried him to his chariot, and took him to the ford of Xanthus, where he vomited blood, briefly recovered, and then lost consciousness again.

l: armour, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: The Danaans exchanged armour so that the most valiant fighters received the best equipment and weaker men received the worse. Once they donned their bronze armour, they marched into battle.

l: shield, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Neptune instructed the Danaans to take the best and largest shields available and to give smaller shields to worse men. Hector's shield and armour were fastened to him when he fell, and Trojan princes held their round shields over him to protect him.

l: spear, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Hector's spear struck Ajax son of Telamon but was stopped by the bands of Ajax's shield and sword. Spears killed or wounded several fighters, including Prothoenor, Promachus, Ilioneus, Satnius, and Hyperenor.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Sleep now departed and went his ways to and fro among mankind,
s: Neptune rallied the Danaans to prevent Hector from taking their ships and covering himself with glory. The battle took place beside the ships and tents, and stones lying under the fighters' feet had been brought to support the ships' sides on the shore.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Jove awakens on Ida, sees Hector wounded and the Trojans driven back, and orders Apollo to restore Hector while Iris tells Neptune to withdraw. Neptune yields after protesting that he is Jove’s equal in honor, and Apollo revives Hector and leads the Trojan counterattack with the aegis. Hector and the Trojans drive the Achaeans back through the trench and set stakes, while Apollo destroys the Achaean wall and opens a broad passage. The Trojans then press toward the Achaean ships as the Achaeans fight desperately under Hector’s assault.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Jove awakens on Ida and sees Hector wounded and the Trojans in confusion while Neptune leads the Achaeans. He orders Iris to make Neptune withdraw and Apollo to restore Hector and drive the Achaeans back, intending that Hector will eventually kill Patroclus and that Achilles will later kill Hector. He answers Nestor’s prayer with thunder as the Trojans renew their attack.

l: Apollo, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Apollo goes to Hector at Jove’s command, restores his strength, and urges him to send the horsemen toward the Achaean ships. He carries Jove’s aegis, panics the Achaeans by shaking it, leads the Trojans forward, kicks down the trench banks, and destroys the Achaean wall.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Hector lies wounded after Ajax strikes him in the chest with a stone, but Apollo restores him to strength. He leads the Trojan advance, kills Stichius and Arcesilaus, and orders the Trojans to press on to the ships while threatening death to any man who holds back.

l: Neptune, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Neptune fights for the Achaeans until Iris delivers Jove’s command that he withdraw. He protests that he and Jove have equal honor and divided realms, but then leaves the field and goes down under the sea.

l: Juno, The Iliad, BOOK XV.
s: Juno denies that she caused Neptune to aid the Achaeans and swears that he acted on his own. She carries Jove’s orders to Iris and Apollo, then tells the gods that Jove’s designs will bring trouble upon mortals and immortals.
